The insect was astonishingly heavy, and, considering everything, I could scarcely blame Jupiter for his opinion of it. But why Legrand agreed with him was something I could not possibly understand.

"I sent for you," he declared pompously when I finished examining the beetle, "so that I could have your advice and assistance in carrying out the intentions of Fate and the bug—"

"My dear Legrand," I interrupted, "you are clearly unwell, and you ought to take some precautions. You must go to bed. I'll stay with you for a few days until this passes. You have a fever and—"

"Take my pulse," he said.

I did so and, to be honest, found not the faintest sign of fever.

"Still, you can be ill without having a fever. Let me prescribe a course of treatment just this once. First, go to bed. Then—"

"You're mistaken," he broke in. "I'm as well as anyone could expect, given my present excitement. If you truly want to help me, you will do something to relieve it."

"And how am I to do that?"

"Very simply. Jupiter and I are making an expedition into the hills on the mainland. We need the help of someone we can rely on, and you're the only person we trust. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me now will subside just the same."

"I'm eager to help you however I can," I replied, "but are you saying this damned beetle has something to do with your expedition into the hills?"

"Yes."

"Then, Legrand, I cannot take part in anything so absurd."

"I'm sorry—extremely sorry—because that means we'll have to attempt it alone."

"Alone! The man must be mad! But wait—how long do you expect to be away?"

"Probably the whole night. We'll leave immediately and, whatever happens, return by sunrise."

"And will you give me your word of honor that once this whim is over, and the business with the bug—good God!—has been settled to your satisfaction, you'll come home and follow my advice without question, as if I were your doctor?"

"Yes, I promise. Now let's go; we have no time to waste."

I accompanied my friend with a heavy heart. We set out at about four o'clock: Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and I. Jupiter brought the scythe and spades, insisting on carrying every one himself. It seemed to me that he did so less from exceptional diligence or helpfulness than from fear of allowing either kind of tool within his master's reach.

"How long I continued in this condition I cannot possibly say. It must have been a considerable interval, however, for when some consciousness of existence returned, dawn was breaking. The balloon floated at an immense elevation above a wilderness of sea, and throughout the enormous compass of the horizon not the slightest trace of land appeared. Yet my sensations upon awakening were by no means as agonizing as one might suppose. Indeed, the composure with which I began examining my circumstances contained more than a hint of approaching madness. I lifted my hands to my eyes in turn, wondering what could have swollen the veins and made the fingernails so frightfully black. Next I inspected my head with care, repeatedly shaking it and feeling over it with close attention, until I convinced myself that it was not, as I had rather strongly suspected, bigger than the balloon. Then, with a knowing air, I searched both pockets of my breeches. Finding my tablets and toothpick case absent, I tried to explain their disappearance, and, failing to do so, became indescribably vexed. At this point I noticed a severe discomfort in my left ankle joint, and a faint awareness of my predicament began to dawn upon me. Strange though it seems, I felt neither amazement nor terror. Whatever emotion I experienced was rather a chuckling delight in the ingenuity I was about to show in escaping this difficulty. Not for an instant did I regard my eventual safety as open to question. For several minutes I remained absorbed in the deepest reflection. I distinctly remember often pursing my lips, laying my forefinger alongside my nose, and indulging in the other gestures and grimaces of men who consider intricate or weighty questions from the comfort of their armchairs. Having assembled my thoughts sufficiently, as I believed, I cautiously and deliberately reached behind my back and released the great iron buckle attached to the waistband of my inexpressibles. Its three teeth were somewhat rusty and moved upon their pivot only with considerable resistance. After some effort, however, I managed to turn them perpendicular to the buckle itself, and was pleased to discover that they held steadily in that position. Taking this improvised implement between my teeth, I next set about loosening the knot of my cravat. Several pauses for rest were necessary before I could perform this operation, but at last I succeeded.

And if he asked why I wanted the information, or thought I had any right to it, I would explain, however little such poor dreams meant to him, that I had loved Estella deeply for a long time. Although I had lost her and must spend my life grieving, anything that concerned her still mattered more to me than anything else in the world. Mr. Jaggers stood completely still and silent through this appeal, apparently unmoved. So I turned to Wemmick. "Wemmick, I know you have a kind heart. I've seen your pleasant home and your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful amusements that give you a rest from business. Please speak to Mr. Jaggers for me. Tell him that, taking everything into account, he ought to be more open with me!"

I have never seen two men exchange stranger looks than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after that speech. At first I feared Wemmick would be fired on the spot. But that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers's expression soften into something like a smile and Wemmick grow more confident.

"What's all this?" Mr. Jaggers said. "You have an old father, and pleasant, playful habits?"

"Well!" Wemmick answered. "If I don't bring them into the office, what difference does it make?"

"Pip," Mr. Jaggers said, placing a hand on my arm and smiling openly, "this man must be the cleverest impostor in London."

"Nothing of the kind," Wemmick replied, bolder still. "I think you're one yourself."

Again they gave each other those curious looks, each apparently still suspecting the other of playing a trick on him.

"You have a pleasant home?" said Mr. Jaggers.

"Since it doesn't interfere with work," Wemmick replied, "let it stay that way. Looking at you now, sir, I wouldn't be surprised if you were planning a pleasant home of your own someday, when you're tired of all this business."

Mr. Jaggers nodded two or three times as if remembering the past, and actually sighed. "Pip," he said, "we won't discuss 'poor dreams.' You know more about those than I do; your experience is much more recent. Now, about the other matter. I'll give you a hypothetical case. Remember, I'm admitting nothing."

He waited until I said I fully understood that he had expressly admitted nothing.

"Now, Pip," Mr. Jaggers continued, "suppose a woman in the circumstances you've described had hidden her child. Suppose she had to tell her legal adviser, after he explained that he needed to know the truth about the child to determine how far he could go in defending her.
